Cutaneous HPV is transcriptionally quiet in skin and carcinoma but productive in warts: a depth-controlled re-mining of public RNA-seq

Short version, formatted to Journal of Investigative Dermatology limits

Authors
Affiliations

Taavi Päll

Institute of Biomedicine and Translational Medicine, University of Tartu

Alla Piirsoo

Institute of Bioengineering, University of Tartu

Marko Piirsoo

Institute of Bioengineering, University of Tartu

Published

October 13, 2026

Abstract

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-papillomaviruses are near-ubiquitous skin commensals, yet whether they are transcriptionally active in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) is unsettled. Because standard pipelines discard the non-human reads carrying viral signal, we re-mined 11,556 public human RNA-seq libraries, typing positives and scoring productive infection from late (L1) capsid transcripts, with cell-line provenance, sequencing depth and library chemistry controlled. HPV signal concentrated in non-primary material: cell-line and engineered libraries were five-fold enriched for positivity (P < 10⁻⁸), dominated by integrated HPV16/HPV18, whereas primary skin carried HPV at 2–4%. Productive infection was abundant in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (93.2% above a control-calibrated floor). cSCC and actinic keratosis, though sequenced four times more deeply, reached that floor in 1.5% of libraries, with median burden six orders of magnitude lower, and were indistinguishable from each other. The deficit was explained neither by depth nor by library chemistry. A minority of carcinoma and keratosis specimens carried genuine productive beta- and alpha-HPV infection. Cutaneous HPV is productive in warts but transcriptionally quiet in healthy skin and carcinoma: a trace, non-productive footprint that any account of beta-HPV in skin cancer must accommodate.

Keywords: human papillomavirus; beta-papillomavirus; cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma; productive infection; contamination

Introduction

Cutaneous beta- and gamma-HPVs act more like normal skin flora than disease-causing pathogens. They are acquired early in life, are ubiquitous in healthy adults, and persist as quiet, low-level infections (Antonsson et al. 2000; Doorbar 2023). At the DNA level, this viral reservoir is large and well-mapped. Shotgun metagenomics detected HPV in 61.3% of healthy skin samples (Ma et al. 2014), while skin swabs found beta-HPV in 92% of adults (Rollison et al. 2019a). This viral community is incredibly diverse, spanning 396 distinct types, 229 of which were previously unknown (Bzhalava et al. 2014). However, these DNA figures alone cannot tell us whether any of this genetic material is actively transcribed.

This question matters because beta-HPV is a suspected cofactor in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), particularly in organ-transplant recipients (Howley and Pfister 2015; Rollison et al. 2019b). Three distinct, mutually compatible theories explain this role using the same data. Under the “hit-and-run” model, beta-HPV works with ultraviolet radiation, immunosuppression or chronic inflammation during early cancer development but becomes dispensable once the tumor forms (Dorfer et al. 2021; Viarisio et al. 2018). Alternatively, the protective-immunity theory suggests T-cell immunity to regular papillomaviruses actively suppresses skin cancer, meaning viral loss reflects immune selection (Lambert et al. 2021; Strickley et al. 2021; Strickley et al. 2019). This idea now includes evidence that viral colonization blocks mutant p53 clone expansion, with beta-HPV disappearing as those clones grow (Son et al. 2025). A third theory requires neither premise, proposing that silence is simply the viral default because the beta-HPV genome uses E8^E2 to repress its own expression, and cell transformation requires inactivating this repressor (Rehm et al. 2022b). Two routes have been proposed for the loss itself: ultraviolet-driven host mutations, for example in p53 or NOTCH, may make the viral oncogenes redundant so that the genome is no longer selected for, and genomic instability under ultraviolet exposure may impair episome replication and segregation between daughter cells (Bruyere et al. 2026). Ultimately, all three models predict declining viral activity from healthy skin to carcinoma, which is why measuring that decline more precisely cannot separate them.

Whether HPV is transcribed in cutaneous carcinoma has been studied directly, and the answers generally converge on “no.” The original cSCC transcriptome study found no viral transcription (Arron et al. 2011). This was mirrored in a study of 12 skin lesions at a median of 66 million reads (Hultin et al. 2019). Similarly, a study of 345 post-transplant tumors at 35 million reads found transcription in only 15 cases (Arroyo Mühr et al. 2021). Another study of 23 risk-stratified biopsies showed zero viral expression, despite a 64% DNA positivity rate (Vandiver et al. 2021). E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization supports these findings, showing expression in just 0.9% of 225 non-anogenital cutaneous SCCs (Fujimoto et al. 2019). The literature is not entirely unanimous, however, as in situ hybridization previously demonstrated EV-HPV transcripts in 4 of 11 PCR-positive transplant cSCCs (Purdie et al. 2005). Critically, what these existing studies lack is a proper denominator. Sample sizes remain small, ranging from only 11 to 345 specimens. Furthermore, four out of five studies looked exclusively at lesions without an unselected-skin comparator. The largest study was limited to formalin-fixed transplant material, and none scored productive replication.

Public archives can supply that missing denominator. Standard pipelines discard non-human reads, but these discarded sequences carry the viral signal (Edgar et al. 2022). This approach has already been successfully applied to skin studies (Bhargava et al. 2025; Leiendecker et al. 2023). However, the method is booby-trapped. HeLa-derived HPV18 contaminates archived data extensively (Adey et al. 2013; Cantalupo et al. 2015; Kazemian et al. 2015). Additionally, sequencing depth and library chemistry both limit what any survey can reliably detect. Here, we re-mine public human RNA-seq data across the entire skin spectrum. We ask at what rate cutaneous HPV is transcribed, which specific types are present, and whether the infection is productive.

Results

HPV signal in public RNA-seq is dominated by non-primary material

Across the unbiased sweep, HPV positivity concentrated in cultured and engineered material: engineered libraries were positive in 9.28% and cell lines in 10.34%, against 2.13% of clinical primary tissue (Table 1), roughly five-fold higher odds for both (engineered OR 4.7, P = 1.5×10⁻⁹; cell line OR 5.3, P = 9.9×10⁻²²). These positives were almost entirely mucosal alpha types. HPV18 met the assignment criterion in 34 libraries cohort-wide, of which 32 were cell lines and none were tissue; HPV16 in 28, of which 24 were cell lines. This is the signature of integrated-HPV lines and their documented contamination of archived data. Genuine primary skin therefore shows detectable HPV transcription in only 2–4% of libraries. Much of the apparent HPV signal in public transcriptomes likely reflects laboratory-derived artifacts, which must be separated out before any prevalence claim.

Viral transcription gives an independent check on that artifact. E1 is thought to be encoded only on polycistronic early mRNAs that also encode E2 (Rehm et al. 2022a; Sankovski et al. 2014), so their counts should track one another unless integration disrupts E2. Cell lines carry integrated HPV DNA and show a median E1:E2 ratio of 129 against 0.27 in productive controls and 0.49 in skin, separating cultured from productive primary infection almost completely (AUC 0.97; Figure 1). Virus-host junction calling confirms it, provided junctions are scored as clustering rather than raw count: raw counts scale with viral load (the two EV libraries have over 12,000 chimeric reads each, spread across about 9,000 sites), whereas integration appears as junctions clustering at a single site. As an independent test of the marker in primary tissue of known progression, we scored a graded HPV16-positive cervical series, where the ratio rises with each grade: the median ratio runs from 0.36 in normal epithelium through 0.78 in high-grade lesion to 2.77 in carcinoma, a 7.7-fold rise (Figure 1 c, plotted on the log2 scale). Late transcription falls away along the same axis. The carcinoma median still sits well below the cell-line median. This fits either a mixture of integrated and episomal genomes or admixture of non-tumor epithelium in a bulk biopsy. The rise in primary tissue suggests that the marker reflects viral integration as a biological process rather than merely culture-derived artifacts.

Skin neoplasia carries trace HPV, not productive infection

Every library, including negatives, was scored as papillomavirus reads per million (RPM). Productive controls (warts, condyloma) reached the control-calibrated detection floor (13.2 RPM) in 93.2% of libraries, and EV biopsies in 80%, with median burdens of 5,408 and 229.6 RPM. Across 406 cSCC/AK libraries only 6 reached it (1.5%), median burden 0.012 RPM, six orders of magnitude lower (Figure 2; Fisher OR 10,183, P = 7.6×10⁻⁹⁹).

This gap is not depth. Neoplasia libraries were sequenced almost four times more deeply than the productive controls (median 45.2M vs 12.2M reads), and depth raised the odds of any HPV read (OR per log₁₀ reads 5.2, P = 5.1×10⁻¹⁴⁴) without raising the odds of reaching the floor, either across groups (OR 1.5, P = 0.49) or within neoplasia alone (OR 1.6, P = 0.7). The deepest cSCC/AK libraries, at 327.3M reads, did not cross it, and the same holds within matched depth bins (Figure S1).

Library chemistry also limits viral recovery, and it too fails to explain the gap. Chemistry was resolved for 6,736 libraries (62.2%) from SRA metadata and construction-protocol text, and its imbalance runs against the negative result: neoplasia is rRNA-depleted in 22.9% of libraries against 7.2% of unselected skin (Table S5), while the productive controls contain none. Adjusting for depth and group, rRNA-depleted libraries were no likelier than poly-A to carry an HPV read (OR 1.0, 95% CI 0.8–1.2), and among the 657 rRNA-depleted libraries alone, not one in either group reached the productive floor.

Pooling actinic keratosis with carcinoma is supported rather than assumed: the 72 AK and 326 cSCC libraries both sit well above unselected skin (trace OR 2.6 and 1.9) and are indistinguishable from each other, depth-adjusted (trace OR 1.4, 0.8–2.3, P = 0.28; floor detection 1/72 against 5/326, Fisher P = 1).

Tissue that cannot host the virus fixes the meaning of that trace. Cutaneous adipose, blood and neural material offer no permissive compartment, yet the 334 such libraries carried a trace HPV read at 28.7%, indistinguishable from the 28% of unselected skin, and not one yielded an assignable type. The background trace rate is the assay’s floor, reproduced where infection is impossible. Decomposing the below-floor libraries by gene puts a mechanism under that floor: 63% of the 230 below-floor skin and neoplasia libraries carry no reads on any HPV gene, and only 13% reach the productive threshold, against 91% of productive controls (Figure S2). Unselected skin, once EV material swept in by the targeted queries is reassigned, forms an almost clean null: 0.1% of 7,800 libraries reach the floor. All principal contrasts were refitted as Bayesian logistic regressions under weakly-informative priors, with concordant results (Table S3).

The transcription program makes the distinction visible (Figure 3). Productive groups run the complete viral program, including the late mRNAs that encode the capsid proteins (L1 in 90% of productive controls, 95.5% of EV; Figure 3 a). Skin and neoplasia are not a truncated program but a uniformly faint one, low across all six frames alike (unselected skin 10.3% for E6, 18.6% for L1). Cell lines are the third shape: E6 and E7 in 90.4% and 93.4% against E2 in 33.8% and L2 in 10.6%. In composition (Figure 3 b), productive controls place 34.9% of viral reads on late genes against 6.4% on the oncogenes; cell lines invert this exactly. Read one library at a time, the same split falls out of the criterion itself, productive controls and EV above the L1 ≥ 3 threshold and skin and neoplasia below (Figure 3 c).

The assay detects genuine productive cutaneous infection where it occurs

Among HPV-positive typed samples, 64% of targeted wart/EV libraries met the L1 criterion against 31.8% of cSCC/AK (OR 3.8, P = 0.013), spanning the expected cutaneous repertoire. A minority of genuine primary-skin lesions carried unambiguous productive infection, most strikingly an HPV12-productive cSCC and two lesions co-infected with the beta types HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage (Table S2); co-infection by two assigned types is itself common enough to tabulate (Table S7). The type landscape is partitioned by population (Figure 4; by type in Table S1, Table S6 and Figure S3): high-risk mucosal HPV16/18 confined almost entirely to cultured material, cutaneous wart and low-risk types in productive controls, the defining beta types in EV, and a beta/gamma reservoir in healthy skin visible mainly below the assignment threshold. Most of the small floor-level excess in neoplasia is attributable to 3 mucosal HPV16 cases the broadened query captured (Table S4); excluding them halves it, to 0.7%.

The reservoir is independently present in public skin DNA

Transcriptional silence of HPV genomes is only informative against a reservoir known to exist, so we re-tabulated a petabase-scale papillomavirus catalog of public metagenome assemblies (Chikhi et al. 2024; Shen et al. 2026) by body site (Methods). Skin metagenomes contribute 1,735 HPV-positive libraries with a cutaneous commensal composition (beta 57.9%, gamma 40.7%, alpha 7.4%), while the same procedure returns the mucosal niche for vaginal metagenomes (alpha 84.5%), so the read-out is not assembly noise (Figure S4). The 14 commonest reservoir types are beta and gamma but for HPV2, and our detection level sees them only as a trace: across our 7,800 unselected-skin libraries they account for 0 assigned and 9 trace detections (Figure 5 a). Across all 130 types the disagreement is general: 102 of the 115 types present in the reservoir are productive in no library here, and HPV2 alone is both abundant in skin DNA and productive in our RNA (Figure 5 b). HPV8, the beta type most often named as the cutaneous carcinoma candidate in serological and DNA studies, is the sharpest case: it is the eighth commonest type in the reservoir, carried by 63 of the 1,735 HPV-positive skin DNA libraries, yet it appears in 0 of the 10,834 RNA libraries screened here, at any level and whether assigned or trace.

Discussion

By re-analyzing reads typically discarded by transcriptomic pipelines, we show that cutaneous HPV is active in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) and quiet in healthy skin. In cSCC and actinic keratosis, it appears only as a trace amount, a presence that increased sequencing depth or improved library chemistry cannot turn into a productive infection.

Against the prior RNA-seq and in situ reports of silence in cutaneous carcinoma (Introduction), our study adds rigorous controls, a clear denominator, and a defined metric. We jointly analyze 406 cSCC/AK libraries and 7,800 unselected-skin libraries in one pipeline. We score productive replication, not just presence, against a baseline of confirmed productive lesions: the same instrument that finds no productive infection in cSCC/AK reports 93.2% productivity in warts.

This result does not settle the mechanism, because all three models predict a declining viral signal along the progression axis. The hit-and-run model works because ultraviolet-induced host mutations can make E6 and E7 dispensable once a tumor is established (Dorfer et al. 2021; Viarisio et al. 2018), after which a genome nothing selects for may be lost from the expanding clone; impaired episome replication and segregation under ultraviolet exposure is a proposed additional route (Bruyere et al. 2026). Protective immunity works because virus-positive cells face negative selection (Son et al. 2025; Strickley et al. 2019). Cis-restriction works because quiescence is the viral default (Rehm et al. 2022b). A fourth consideration is not a model but a property of the readout: late transcription requires terminal differentiation (Doorbar et al. 2012), so a poorly differentiated tumor cannot run the late program regardless. Our trace decomposition answers it, since 63% of below-floor skin and neoplasia libraries carry no reads on any HPV gene at all, not merely no late ones (Figure S2). Our data measure this exact axis and cannot separate the three models. Nor does absent transcription imply clearance: episomal genomes may persist silently, or with intermittent activity, below the detection limit of bulk RNA sequencing. Absent productive transcription in established lesions does not exclude a transient viral contribution earlier in carcinogenesis.

The elevated beta-HPV activity that Son and colleagues found in keratinocyte clones of sun-exposed skin (Son et al. 2025) does not conflict with our quiet reservoir, because we sequenced whole biopsies without sorting for ultraviolet exposure. A signal arising from small keratinocyte clones is diluted when averaged across an entire biopsy, a documented effect for cutaneous HPV (Purdie et al. 2005). We nevertheless agree on viral presence: we recovered trace HPV from 62.5% of AK libraries. HPV8 itself, however, was absent at any level from all 10,834 analyzed RNA libraries. That absence argues against persistent productive HPV8 transcription in established lesions while remaining compatible with transient, focal or latent activity. The nine-valent vaccine reduced the burden of actinic keratosis in a randomized trial (Wenande et al. 2025). It targets mucosal alpha types, not the resident beta reservoir, so any protective effect likely depends on cross-reactive or non-specific immunity.

The rare productive infections we do find are beta-HPV, which constrains how the trace result should be read. Outside warts and EV, three primary-skin lesions carry unambiguous productive infection: an HPV12-productive cSCC, and two actinic-keratosis/cSCC libraries co-infected with HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage and high depth. HPV12, HPV96 and HPV182 belong to the beta-HPV species Betapapillomavirus 1, 5 and 2, respectively, so the genus running a complete productive program in these lesions is the same genus the cofactor debate concerns. Productive beta-HPV infection of primary skin is therefore possible and simply rare. The silence we report in cutaneous neoplasia is thus not a ceiling on what beta-HPV can do in skin. No productive HPV12, HPV96 or HPV182 has to our knowledge been described from public RNA-seq of primary skin.

A 2–4% active transcription rate does not contradict a 90% viral DNA reservoir. Three factors reconcile this gap. First, beta-HPV DNA loads sit below one copy per 60 cells (Weissenborn et al. 2012), falling beneath the detection limit of bulk RNA sequencing. Second, the tissue sources differ: skin epidemiology studies test surface swabs and hair bulbs (92% and 73% prevalence) (Rollison et al. 2019a), while RNA-seq uses deep biopsies that miss surface and hair follicle layers. Third, screening panels miss 229 skin types lacking reference genomes (Bzhalava et al. 2014). DNA data confirm that the general reservoir differs from tumor-driving viruses: fewer than 5% of skin types match later cSCC (Rollison et al. 2021), and paired eyebrow hair and cSCC showed only 9.1% genotype concordance in another cohort (Oh et al. 2026).

Unadjusted analyses are dominated by contamination. Cultured materials show a five-fold enrichment that reflects known HeLa cell contamination in archives (Adey et al. 2013; Cantalupo et al. 2015; Kazemian et al. 2015), traced in one facility to a quality-control cell pool run with tumors (Selitsky et al. 2020). Over 65% of viral sequences from 712 libraries group with reagents or protocols instead of actual specimens (Asplund et al. 2019), and re-analyses have invalidated major archive-scale microbial findings (Gihawi et al. 2023). Our safeguards are not individually new (Cantalupo and Pipas 2019); our contribution is quantifying the size of each artifact rather than merely asserting it.

Petabase-scale surveys are now the standard method for establishing viral presence across body sites, but a presence catalog cannot measure biological activity. Because these surveys rely on sequence assembly, integrated genomes fail to assemble across the virus-host junction. The viral genome state must be inferred from individual reads or transcription rather than catalog membership alone. For example, conditioning data on near-complete L1-anchored contigs yields an intact E2 gene in 99.3% of cervical carcinoma contigs compared to 99.9% in skin (Table S8). This approaches a tautology, as the completeness criterion itself selects for episomal genomes in both tissues.

Several limitations affect these findings, starting with the non-random nature of archival sampling, which makes the absolute healthy-skin rate an estimate. Sequencing chemistry could only be resolved for 62.2% of libraries, while input amount, RNA integrity, and fragment selection are entirely unrecoverable from the archived metadata. Because biopsy averaging dilutes focal transcription, our productivity estimates are a conservative lower bound. Finally, because tissue and diagnosis labels are programmatic and imperfect, viral typing is constrained by the reference panel, and the data are cross-sectional, these results describe productive-status phenomenology rather than prove a definitive mechanism.

Ultimately, cutaneous HPV is productive in warts and epidermodysplasia verruciformis, but leaves only a trace, non-productive footprint in cutaneous squamous neoplasia, regardless of sequencing depth or library chemistry. This phenotype is the baseline any theory of beta-HPV in skin cancer must address. Because all major hypotheses predict this outcome, more precise measurement of viral activity will not separate them. That requires study designs that break the shared prediction. Crucial approaches include matched DNA and RNA profiling across the precursor-to-carcinoma transition, precise spatial resolution of residual viral particles relative to mutant clones and infiltrating T cells, and ongoing interventional studies. While single-cell resolution has already been demonstrated in cutaneous lesions (Devitt et al. 2019), the critical next step is applying this technology at a cohort scale across the actinic-keratosis-to-carcinoma transition.

Materials and Methods

Full details are given in Supplementary Materials and Methods.

Pipeline and reference panel. A Nextflow workflow screened each library for papillomavirus reads with Kraken2 against a combined human/HPV database, typed positives against the complete PaVE reference set (455 sequences) by STAR alignment, and classified early versus late viral transcripts. Code and configuration are available as stated in the Data Availability Statement.

Cohort. Public human RNA-seq runs were discovered through NCBI Entrez and assembled into a case/control design spanning productive controls (warts, condyloma), epidermodysplasia verruciformis, cutaneous neoplasia (cSCC, actinic keratosis), an unselected-skin null, and cell-line, engineered and non-permissive-tissue comparators. Group assignment read curated SRA metadata, with a small override table correcting studies whose submitted metadata is absent or misleading. 11,556 libraries were screened.

Whole-library screening. Every library was screened in full: no step subsamples reads and fasterq-dump was run without a spot limit. This matters because reads deposited from a coordinate-sorted alignment emerge from the SRA in reference order, placing unmapped, and therefore viral, reads at the end of the run. Reads reaching the screen were a median 98.6% of the SRA-reported spot count, with per-group medians spanning 95.8% to 99.5%, so no group was read less completely than another.

Calling infection and productivity. A reference was assigned when coverage breadth was at least 0.10 and mean depth at least 2. Every library, including negatives, was scored as RPM, the depth-normalized burden used throughout. Productive infection required at least three L1 major-capsid reads, and a control-calibrated detection floor was set at the 5th-percentile RPM of non-cell-line productive controls (13.2 RPM).

Confounder control and statistics. Sequencing depth entered every model as log10 library size. Library-selection chemistry was recovered from SRA LibrarySelection and, where that field is generic, from library-construction protocol text, resolving 62.2% of libraries. Integration was read from the E1:E2 transcript ratio and validated against virus-host junctions and an independent graded cervical series. Logistic regressions and Fisher exact tests were fitted in R, with Wilson intervals for proportions and a Bayesian re-analysis under weakly-informative priors as a robustness check.

Ethics Statement

This study analyzed only publicly archived, de-identified human sequencing data retrieved from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive, and generated no new human or animal material. Institutional review board approval and informed consent were therefore not required for the work reported here. Ethical approval and participant consent for the primary studies were the responsibility of their submitting investigators and are recorded in the corresponding BioProject entries.

Data Availability Statement

The complete analysis pipeline, comprising the Nextflow workflow, the per-process software environments and container definitions, the reference-construction and SRA-discovery scripts, and the downstream R analysis and statistical-inference code, is openly available at https://github.com/tpall/hpv-human-skin. All sequencing data analyzed here are public and were obtained from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive; the per-cohort lists of accessions (SRR/SRX), with assigned tissue category, diagnosis, and cell-line/engineered annotations, are provided as Supplementary Data. Reference genomes were retrieved from the Papillomavirus Episteme (PaVE; https://pave.niaid.nih.gov) and NCBI RefSeq. No new sequencing data were generated.

Supplementary Materials and Methods

Methods

Overview and implementation

All analyses were performed with a custom, portable workflow implemented in Nextflow DSL2 (≥23.04; Di Tommaso et al. (2017)) and run on an HPC cluster under the SLURM scheduler. Each step runs in an isolated, version-pinned software environment specified per process as both a Conda environment.yml and an OCI container image; the exact container build was used for execution, and the versions quoted below are those pinned by the container tags. Default parameter values are given in parentheses and were used unless stated otherwise.

The workflow comprises a one-time reference-construction stage followed by a per-sample pipeline: SRA discovery → FASTQ download → quality control → Kraken2 papillomavirus screen → branch on HPV status (only HPV-positive libraries proceed) → STAR alignment to the HPV reference panel → coverage-based HPV typing → early/late transcript classification → aggregation and reporting.

HPV reference panel and Kraken2 database

A cutaneous-inclusive HPV reference panel was assembled from the Papillomavirus Episteme (PaVE 2.0; Van Doorslaer et al. (2017)). Because PaVE 2.0 exposes no bulk-FASTA endpoint, genomes were enumerated through its REST API (GET /api/genome?limit=9999&includeNonRef=true, which includes non-reference candidate genomes), filtered to human-host entries (host_common_name == "human"), and retrieved individually (GET /api/genome/{locus_id}), with each genome sequence taken from the returned itemSequence. Reference-quality complete HPV genomes from NCBI RefSeq were added on a best-effort basis via Entrez Direct (≥16.2; "Human papillomavirus"[Organism] AND refseq[filter] AND complete genome[Title]). Sequences were concatenated and deduplicated by identifier (seqkit ≥2.5; Shen et al. (2016)) to yield the final panel (hpv_all.fasta; n = 455 genomes spanning the alpha, beta, gamma, mu and nu genera plus unclassified candidate types; the panel is built at setup from live PaVE/RefSeq queries and its exact composition depends on build date). A per-type genus lookup was derived from the PaVE ICTV taxonomy array. Gene models for the eight protein-coding ORFs of interest (E1, E2, E4, E5, E6, E7, L1, L2) were extracted from each genome’s PaVE feature annotation, with multi-segment features collapsed to a single span, and written as a GFF3 annotation used downstream for transcript classification.

A STAR genome index was built over the panel (STAR ≥2.7.10; --genomeSAindexNbases 6 for the small viral genomes). A Kraken2 database (≥2.1.3; Wood et al. (2019)) was constructed from the NCBI taxonomy and the human reference library (GRCh38), to which all panel HPV genomes were added under a Papillomaviridae taxon, so that human and HPV reads are jointly classified and HPV reads are resolved within the papillomavirus clade.

Dataset assembly and SRA discovery

Public human RNA-seq libraries were identified by programmatic query of the NCBI Sequence Read Archive through Entrez (Biopython Bio.Entrez; pysradb/Biopython container 2.2.1), with every query intersected with a common base filter ("Homo sapiens"[Organism] AND "RNA-Seq"[Strategy] AND "public"[Access]). We used three complementary discovery strategies, corresponding to the case/control framing of the study. An unbiased prevalence sweep of human skin and related tissues (the prevalence cohort) estimated baseline HPV-positivity rates in tissue not selected for infection. A targeted productive-lesion query (epidermodysplasia verruciformis, verruca/warts, condyloma) provided positive controls of known productive cutaneous HPV infection. A broadened skin-neoplasia query additionally captured cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, actinic keratosis and Bowen disease alongside the wider wart/papilloma vocabulary, to interrogate HPV across the AK-to-cSCC setting.

For each retrieved run, metadata were parsed into a per-run samplesheet (one row per SRR). A tissue category was assigned by longest-keyword-first matching of sample title and source fields against a curated keyword table, yielding one of four classes: skin, anogenital, oral, or unclassified (the default, meaning no site keyword was present rather than a site outside the other three). Keywords are matched with letter boundaries on both sides, tolerating a plural suffix, so that a keyword is not matched inside an unrelated word; the boundary is letter-based rather than word-based because SRA free text routinely separates tokens with underscores and digits. Squamous- and basal-cell-carcinoma abbreviations are exempt from the boundary rule, since they legitimately take anatomical affixes (cSCC, RDEB-SCC, SCCIS). A free-text diagnosis was extracted against a fixed pathology vocabulary (carcinoma, SCC, BCC, keratosis, wart, verruca, condyloma, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, dysplasia/CIN, normal/healthy/control, and similar terms), defaulting to “unspecified”. Library layout (single- vs paired-end) was taken from the SRA record. To enable robust downstream parsing, comma-containing free-text fields were retained in a raw samplesheet and stripped from the slim samplesheet consumed by the workflow.

Read download and quality control

FASTQ files were retrieved from the SRA (Leinonen et al. 2011) with the NCBI SRA Toolkit (3.1.1, pinned; later 3.4.x builds were unstable in our environment) by prefetch followed by fasterq-dump --split-3, and compressed with pigz. Reads were quality- and adapter-trimmed with fastp (0.23.4; Chen et al. (2018)) using a minimum qualified base quality of Phred 20 (--qualified_quality_phred 20) and a minimum retained read length of 36 nt (--length_required 36); paired-end libraries additionally used --detect_adapter_for_pe. Per-sample failures (withdrawn accessions, network errors) were tolerated by a fail-soft retry-then-ignore policy so that a single unavailable run did not abort a batch. Every library was screened in full: no step subsamples reads, and fasterq-dump was run without a spot limit. This matters more than it may appear, because reads deposited from a coordinate-sorted alignment emerge from the SRA in reference order, which places unmapped, and therefore viral, reads at the end of the run; screening only the leading portion of such a library would miss the signal entirely and would do so non-randomly. As a check on the whole path from download to classification, the reads reaching the Kraken2 screen correspond to a median 98.6% of the SRA-reported spot count across the 10,834 screened libraries (5th percentile 85.5%), the small shortfall being fastp quality and length filtering, and the per-group medians span 95.8% to 99.5%, so no sample group was read less completely than another.

HPV screening and positivity calling

Trimmed reads were classified against the combined human+HPV Kraken2 database (≥2.1.3, paired or single mode as appropriate). HPV-classified reads were enumerated as the count of unique read identifiers assigned to the Papillomaviridae family or any papillomavirus genus/type taxon. A library was called HPV-positive when its HPV read count met or exceeded a threshold of 10 reads (hpv_min_reads = 10), and HPV-negative otherwise; HPV-negative libraries were recorded for rate estimation but proceeded no further. HPV-classified reads from positive libraries were extracted (seqtk 1.4), keeping paired mates in register, for targeted alignment. This split, in which every screened library contributes to positivity rates but only positives advance to typing, is the central branch point of the workflow.

HPV typing

HPV reads from positive libraries were aligned to the HPV reference panel with STAR (2.7.11b; Dobin et al. (2013)) in an end-to-end, splice-disabled configuration appropriate for compact viral genomes (--alignIntronMax 1, --alignEndsType EndToEnd, --outFilterMismatchNmax 3), permitting up to 50 multi-mapping locations (--outFilterMultimapNmax 50) to accommodate the high sequence similarity among HPV types. Sorted, indexed BAMs were summarized per reference with samtools coverage (samtools 1.21; Danecek et al. (2021)) at a minimum mapping quality of 10. For each reference we recorded read count, covered bases, coverage breadth (fraction of the reference covered ≥1×) and mean depth. A reference was assigned to a sample when it satisfied both coverage breadth ≥ 0.10 (hpv_min_coverage) and mean depth ≥ 2 (hpv_min_depth); the full per-reference coverage table was retained regardless of assignment. The dual breadth-and-depth criterion guards against spurious assignment from a few reads piling up on a short, conserved region.

Early/late transcript classification

To distinguish productive from non-productive infection, reads from each HPV-positive alignment were assigned to viral genes with featureCounts (subread ≥2.0; Liao et al. (2014)) against the PaVE-derived gene annotation (-t gene -g gene_name, minimum overlap 20 nt, minimum mapping quality 10; pairing detected directly from the BAM and counted as read pairs when applicable). Per-gene counts were aggregated into an early total (E1, E2, E4, E5, E6, E7) and a late total (L1, L2). An infection was classified as productive when the L1 (major-capsid) read count reached the late-transcript threshold of 3 (late_transcript_min_reads = 3). Productivity was gated on L1 specifically, rather than on combined L1+L2 signal, because L1 capsid expression is the more stringent marker of virion-producing late-stage infection, whereas isolated L2 signal can arise from low-level transcription or cross-mapping; this single rule was applied uniformly across all samples and run batches.

Cell-line, engineered, and contaminant flagging

Because public RNA-seq is heavily populated by cancer cell lines, many carrying integrated HPV (e.g. HeLa/HPV18) that is a well-documented source of spurious HPV signal in archived data (Cantalupo et al. 2015; Kazemian et al. 2015), every sample was annotated along three independent axes from its metadata using a shared pattern library: is_cell_line (named lines such as HeLa, SiHa, CaSki, HaCaT, A431, plus generic markers like “cell line”, “immortalized”, “passage n”, ATCC/DSMZ accessioning, PDX/xenograft), is_engineered (shRNA/siRNA/sgRNA, CRISPR/Cas9, transduction/transfection, lentiviral and plasmid-backbone constructs), and is_in_vitro (cultured but non-immortalized material such as primary keratinocytes/fibroblasts/melanocytes, NHEK, organotypic/raft cultures, organoids, and differentiation time-courses). Explicit “primary” annotations were treated as non-cell-line. These flags annotate rather than exclude samples, so that cell-line positives are retained as positive controls but can be separated from primary-tissue signal at analysis. For the prevalence-sweep cohort, study-level heuristic calls were additionally refined by manual curation through a structured workbook, with precedence sample > study > heuristic, and a provenance label recorded for each overridden call. As a further contaminant guard, low-coverage-breadth assignments (breadth < 0.15) and alpha-genus/HPV16/HPV18 calls were tabulated by study to surface project-level contamination.

Cohort framing and depth-normalized burden analysis

Because lesional libraries may simply be sequenced more deeply than unselected skin, raw HPV read counts confound infection burden with sequencing depth. To neutralize this, every Kraken2-screened library, including HPV-negative ones, was scored as papillomavirus reads per million (RPM), computed from the Kraken2 report as the Papillomaviridae clade read count divided by the sum of unclassified and root-level clade reads, times 10⁶. Samples were assigned to mutually exclusive sample groups in fixed precedence: cell_line (any cell-line flag), EV (epidermodysplasia verruciformis diagnosis), control_productive (wart/condyloma), neoplasia (squamous/carcinoma/SCC/keratosis/Bowen), contamination_study (pre-specified contaminated studies), unselected_skin (skin tissue), and other.

Because these rules read free-text SRA metadata, they mis-file the minority of studies whose submitted metadata is absent or actively misleading. Three such cases were identified by inspecting every library that reached the detection floor, and corrected through a curated override table (assets/tier_overrides.csv) in which each row records the accession, the corrected field, and the evidence. (i) A ten-library cohort of epidermodysplasia verruciformis patient skin biopsies (Saeidian et al. 2023) carries only tissue=Skin in its per-run metadata, so the diagnosis vocabulary never sees “verruciformis”; these were moved to the EV group, which otherwise contained only immortalized EV culture models (retained under cell_line). (ii) Six libraries from a study of HPV31-positive HaCaT (HaCaT31) cells expose only a knockdown label and skin in their parsed fields, so no cell-line pattern can fire; the cell-line flag was set. (iii) One primary cutaneous wart carried a submitter sample label in the SRA cell_line attribute and was wrongly flagged as a line; the flag was cleared, returning it to control_productive. Together these corrections move 16 of 11,282 screened libraries.

Two further sets of libraries were excluded outright rather than regrouped, because neither a null nor a control describes them. First, 433 16S rRNA amplicon libraries: an amplicon library carries no HPV sequence that could be detected whatever the infection status, so these are structural zeros rather than negative observations, and leaving them in would deflate the background rate every comparison is measured against. Second, fifteen libraries annotated source_name=Skin or mucosa, tissue=adjacent mucosal tissues, which are the matched adjacent tissue of five condyloma acuminatum donors, each sequenced as an RNA-seq library plus a MeRIP input and IP fraction. Tissue taken millimeters from a productive lesion cannot separate independent infection from spillover out of that lesion, so a detection there is not evidence of virus in the absence of disease, and five donors in three fractions each is one comparison rather than a population. Their lesions are retained in control_productive, so neither the productive contrast nor the detection floor calibrated on it is affected. The analyzed cohort is therefore 10,834 libraries. The same is_cell_line corrections are applied to the positivity model, so that sample-class definitions are identical across models. Running the pipeline with the override table disabled reproduces the uncorrected group assignment exactly, and both outputs are retained. A control-calibrated detection floor was defined as the 5th-percentile RPM of non-cell-line productive controls (warts/condyloma); libraries below this floor were considered “not detected at control level”. To show that any group difference was not an artifact of depth, the fraction of libraries at or above the detection floor was additionally computed within matched total-read bins (<5M, 5–10M, 10–20M, 20–40M, >40M). The same per-sample table also yielded an HPV-type × sample-group catalog. This analysis pooled the lesion cohorts against the prevalence-sweep null and used the curated cell-line flags. Logistic-regression models (positivity by sample class; productive-level detection by sample group with a log10 sequencing-depth covariate) and Fisher exact tests were fitted in R; Wilson intervals are reported for proportions. As a robustness check, the positivity, depth-controlled detection and productivity models were additionally refitted as Bayesian logistic regressions with explicit weakly-informative priors, namely Normal(0, 2.5) on the log-odds coefficients and Normal(0, 5) on the intercept, applied directly to the log-odds scale rather than as flat or improper defaults, using rstanarm (Goodrich et al. 2024) (four Markov chains of 2,000 iterations; convergence confirmed by \(\hat{R} \le 1.004\) with no divergent transitions). Effects are summarized by the posterior median odds ratio, its 95% credible interval, and the posterior probability of a positive effect; the near-separated productive-controls-versus-skin contrast was additionally checked under a heavier-tailed Student-t(3) prior (Table S3).

Library-selection chemistry

Sequencing depth bounds what a viral-transcript survey can detect, and RNA-selection chemistry bounds it in a second, independent way: poly-A capture recovers polyadenylated early transcripts efficiently but is inefficient for the rest of the viral pool, so two libraries of equal depth need not have equal power to detect HPV. Chemistry was therefore looked up for every library in the burden analysis and entered alongside depth. SRA RunInfo LibrarySelection was fetched for the exact accession set already analyzed, with no fresh search, so the cohort is unchanged (bin/fetch_library_selection.py). That field is authoritative where it carries a specific value (“PolyA”, “Oligo-dT”, “Inverse rRNA”, “RANDOM”) but is the generic “cDNA” for 74.6% of libraries, so the free-text LIBRARY_CONSTRUCTION_PROTOCOL and DESIGN_DESCRIPTION records were fetched in a second pass and matched against curated poly-A and rRNA-depletion phrase sets (bin/classify_library_chemistry.py). Libraries whose text supports both calls, or neither, are held at unspecified rather than assigned, and the amplification chemistries that are neither selection (3’-barcoded droplet libraries, SMART template-switching) are kept as their own levels rather than pooled with poly-A capture. This resolved chemistry for 6,736 of 10,834 libraries (62.2%).

The two-source procedure is necessary rather than merely convenient, and the graded cervical validation series is the demonstration: every one of its libraries is filed in SRA as LibrarySelection = cDNA, while its construction protocol reads “Ribosomal RNA was deleted”. Run as a blind test, the classifier recovers rRNA depletion for 15/15 of them from protocol text alone, which is also the independent confirmation that the series is rRNA-depleted rather than poly-A-selected.

Integration status: E1:E2 transcript ratio and virus–host junctions

Integration of a papillomavirus genome disrupts the E2 open reading frame, which represses E6 and E7. Because E1 and E2 are encoded on the same early transcript, their read counts track one another unless that disruption has occurred, so their ratio reports integration from the transcript classification already computed for every library. Libraries with at least five combined E1 and E2 reads were scored as log2((E1 + 0.5)/(E2 + 0.5)); separation between groups was quantified as the area under the ranked ratio and by Wilcoxon rank-sum test. A ratio is undefined where integration has proceeded to the point that the early region is lost apart from E6 and E7, since E1 and E2 are then both silent. Those libraries were called by a second criterion: at least five combined E6 and E7 reads, fewer than five combined E1 and E2 reads, and no more than 5% of viral reads assigned to L1 or L2, which is the integrated-carcinoma pattern of oncogene transcription without a late program. A library was called integration-like if either criterion fired; the two are reported separately because the first is blind to the material the second detects.

The ratio was validated against direct evidence of integration in a subset of 17 libraries spanning its range. Reads were aligned with STAR (Dobin et al. 2013) to a combined index of GRCh38 and the HPV reference panel, with chimeric detection enabled (--chimSegmentMin 20, --chimJunctionOverhangMin 15), and chimeric junctions were retained when one side fell on an HPV contig and the other on a human chromosome. Integration was scored not by the number of such junctions, which scales with viral depth and is largest in episomal libraries, but by their clustering: the fraction of a library’s junctions falling at its single most-supported coordinate pair, since a genuine integration yields one recurrent junction whereas chimeric-read artifacts are scattered. Observed values were bimodal with an empty interval between 0.00–0.03 and 0.33–0.46, and a threshold of 0.2 was placed within it. The limit of a negative call was set empirically rather than by model: integration was called in a library carrying as few as 2,776 HPV reads, which bounds the viral depth at which absence is informative.

The ratio was validated externally on a graded cervical series (BioProject PRJNA612785, study SRP252916): HPV-negative normal cervical epithelium, HPV16-positive normal epithelium, HPV16-positive high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and HPV16-positive squamous carcinoma, six cases per arm, all paired-end and rRNA-depleted rather than poly(A)-selected. Libraries were typed with the same pipeline and scored with the same criteria and thresholds as the skin cohort, with the study’s own design arms supplied in place of the group assignment (bin/e1e2_integration_marker.R --groups), so the marker was evaluated against labels it had no part in assigning. Single-cell and single-nucleus libraries are excluded from the marker by default throughout, since 3’-biased barcoded coverage cannot support a ratio across the early region; truncating such libraries does not remedy this, so they are dropped rather than downsampled.

Independent DNA reservoir from public metagenomes

The presence axis against which the transcriptional result is read comes from a published petabase-scale papillomavirus catalog rather than from our own pipeline. Shen et al. screened the Logan assembly of 27 million archived sequencing libraries (Chikhi et al. 2024) for papillomavirus contigs by profile-HMM detection of the conserved L1 B and I domains and clustered them into operational types (Shen et al. 2026); we re-tabulated their released cluster-by-library table by body site. Libraries were bucketed by the BioSample organism field into skin (human skin metagenome, skin metagenome), vaginal and gut metagenomes. The skin taxon also carries environmental transit surfaces and non-human animal skin, which were removed with a curated run exclusion list built from BioSample attributes (bin/build_skin_run_exclusions.py). Each contig cluster was mapped to an HPV type through the study’s own taxonomy demarcation table and then to a genus through the same type-to-genus map used for our RNA catalogs, so the two modalities are labeled identically; a cluster with a papillomavirus identity that resolves to no genus is reported as Unresolved and one with no reference match as Novel.

All quantities from this catalog are compositions conditional on positivity: the denominator is the HPV-positive libraries of a body site, and a library carrying types of two genera contributes to both, so genus proportions within a site do not sum to one. No prevalence is computed from the catalog, since a defensible denominator would require the screened-library count per body site to be reconstructed under the same freeze applied to the numerator. The type-level comparison against our own data joins the reservoir types onto both RNA catalogs, the assigned catalog (Table S1) and the trace catalog (Table S6, at least five best-hit reads, MAPQ ≥ 20, and a majority of the library’s primary alignments on that reference), so that a type below the assignment threshold in skin RNA is reported as a trace detection and never as an absence. This tabulation is implemented in dna_rna_triangulation/shen_reservoir_by_tissue.R and dna_rna_triangulation/skin_dna_vs_rna_corrected.R, and Figure 5 is built from their outputs by manuscript/figure_reservoir.R.

Execution at scale

For cohorts of thousands of libraries, a chunked driver processed the samplesheet in fixed-size batches (default 100 libraries per chunk). After each successful chunk, per-sample outputs (Kraken2 reports, HPV typing and transcript tables, and HPV status) were aggregated and the chunk’s working directory was deleted to bound disk use; a failed chunk was left intact for inspection and resumed on rerun. A single combined report was generated over the aggregated outputs at completion. Summary tables and figures were produced in R (tidyverse), and the depth-normalized burden analysis was implemented as a standalone R script operating on the aggregated Kraken2 reports, typing tables, and curated sample flags.

Supplementary Figures and Tables

Above-floor HPV in tissue that cannot host it: two contaminated studies

The non-permissive tissue group is defined by biology, not by its HPV content, so it also exposes the opposite case: libraries from non-permissive material that carry HPV above the trace level. Two studies do, and both were held out of the control group for that reason.

SRP572742 (skeletal muscle and blood from myotonic dystrophy patients, n = 66) is HPV-positive at any level in 83% of libraries, with 3 crossing the control-calibrated detection floor and a maximum of 5.3 RPM. Neither muscle nor blood contains stratified squamous epithelium, so no part of that signal can be infection of the sampled tissue.

SRP565659 makes the point under internal control. It is a multi-omic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma study in which skin and peripheral blood were taken from the same patients and sequenced together (Table S1 of the source publication assigns every run a tissue). Its 26 skin libraries are strongly HPV-positive, 88% at any level and up to 12.0 RPM, as expected for lesional skin. Its 42 blood and lymph-node libraries (same patients, same runs, tissue that cannot host the virus) are HPV-positive at 52%, up to 3.6 RPM, with one library above the floor.

The pattern in both is a minority of reads appearing in libraries with no biological source for them, alongside co-sequenced libraries carrying a genuine high-titre signal. That is the signature of index hopping and inter-library carry-over rather than infection, and it is the same phenomenon that makes cell-line contamination the dominant driver of apparent HPV positivity in public transcriptomes. Two consequences follow for how the trace signal should be read. First, a non-zero HPV read count in a single library is not evidence of infection even when the tissue is plausible, which is why the analysis here is anchored on a control-calibrated floor rather than on detection. Second, studies whose design places high-titre and HPV-free material in the same sequencing run will inflate apparent prevalence in the HPV-free arm, so prevalence estimates drawn from public data without a non-permissive control are upper bounds.
